voice_event.text:
Three things, and the first is the one that reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - not a saying to be studied but an order to be obeyed. The one we remember as first among us walked into church one day and heard those words read, took them as though they had been said to him alone, and before the day was over had given away the land he had inherited. Not long after that, hearing the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - he gave away the rest as well, placed his sister with women he trusted who were already given to a life of virginity, and began the discipline himself.

The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but, being the same, took a human body for the salvation and well-being of man, so that having shared in human birth he might make man share in the divine nature - that is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so: read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come upon earth for the salvation of men.

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it arose; the knowledge of God spread; and death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything - which is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer offered us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten: his coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

results.message: You mentioned him being obeyed. Did any of them write about him with affection?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We did not leave behind letters of devotion or prayers of longing addressed to him the way later ages did - that is not the form our record takes. What we left instead is shorter and harder: a verse taken up to answer a struggle, a saying given to redirect a disciple, the Psalms recited through the day alongside our work. The affection, if you can call it that, shows in what a person was willing to give up when those words were heard. One of us gave away inherited land in two separate visits to the church, never went back for it, and then disappeared for years inside an abandoned fort with its entrance built up, while people gathered outside anyway just to be near a wall with someone praying behind it. To most people that looked like throwing a life away. We understood it as the opposite - the only way left, once dying for the faith was no longer asked of anyone, to give the whole of a life rather than a part of it.

So the affection is there, but you will not find it in the words themselves so much as in what following him cost and what that cost was counted worth. We kept his commands, not poems about keeping them. That is the shape love took among us.

results.message: What role did women have in your tradition?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We will not pretend this was common ground for us. Most of what survives in our own voice about discernment and authority is attributed to men. But women did hold the same discipline, and they were remembered for it.

One of the greatest among us, Pachomius, when his own sister came to him wanting the same life, cut her hair, put a girdle around her, and made a dwelling-place for her alone on the opposite side of the river at the distance of a mile. That was not an isolated case. The tradition tells of women living alone in cells, women living in shared houses, women trusted with real responsibility - one woman, Talida of Antinoe, is remembered leading sixty virgins on the path she had chosen, and another, Taor, living withdrawn from ordinary commerce in a way the men among us would have recognized as their own. And when the archbishop of Alexandria was on the run from the Arians, he did not go to his kinsmen or his friends or the clergy - he went to a young woman living as a virgin, and she hid him, washed his feet, saw to what he needed, and borrowed books and brought them to him, and nobody in Alexandria knew where he was for the whole of that time.

The record keeper who wrote those lives down said plainly that God gave women an equal measure of strength of will as he gave to men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of the labour of ascetic excellence. He said it. And then he waited until the thirty-fifth chapter to write about them, after thirty-four chapters of men.

What we can tell you honestly is this: named women's sayings survive, and so do about fifteen narrated lives of named women, several carrying their reported speech - the same third-person form in which this material narrates its men, by the same author, at the same length. What is missing is narrower than a missing genre: it is a woman's own first-person account, which this material does not have from anyone. The women are there. They are not there in their own voices the way the men are in theirs - not in what survives to us. That is the shape of the silence, and we will not fill it.

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
If you mean the woman who hid the archbishop - the virgin of Alexandria who kept Athanasius safe while the Arians were moving against him - we know this much. Palladius, the one who wrote her story down, says he saw her himself and took her to be about seventy years old when he met her. The clergy testified about her: that at twenty she had been so beautiful that people stared, and that she had withdrawn from sight for exactly that reason, so as not to be the occasion of anyone's stumbling. When Athanasius came to her at midnight, fleeing, she hid him, washed his feet, saw to what he needed, and borrowed books and brought them to him. Nobody in Alexandria knew where he was for the whole of that time. When it was over he appeared suddenly in the church and explained himself to the people: he had not come to them because he did not want to put them in the position of having to swear false oaths, and he had gone to the one person no one could suspect him of going to, because she was young and beautiful. He said he had gained two things by it, his own life and hers.

What we do not know: her name. Whether she had family, or means of her own, or lived supported by the church. Whether she ever spoke of what it cost her to be that beautiful and that withdrawn. Whether anyone came to her afterward for counsel the way they came to our honored elders. Palladius saw her and the clergy knew her story, but that is where the thread ends. We will not invent what is missing.

voice_event.text:
It is not effort alone, and we said so at length. The question was put to us directly - if a man strives with all his might for a good result, can he become master of what is good? - and the answer that started the argument was no, not unless he has it as a gift. Grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony; we thought we ought to have both alike. We argued it from cases rather than from principles. Paul was drawn to salvation while he was eager for bloodshed, and Matthew while he was at his taking of taxes - neither was reaching for it. But Zacchaeus, and the thief on the cross, by their own desires brought violence to bear on the kingdom of heaven. Neither pattern was made to govern the other.

What we would say plainly is that the main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work; and sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand. We took that from experience rather than from argument - led, as we put it, not by chattering words but by experience.

We should tell you honestly that some things you might expect us to have argued, we did not. Were people born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin? No letter and no story we kept speaks to it in so many words. What we did argue was this: the main share belongs to grace, not to our own works - but both are real, and neither one makes the other disappear.

results.message: Earlier you talked about the heart. Does that connect to what you just said about grace?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
There was another voice among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. Where our most systematic teacher had the mind clear itself until it beheld its own proper radiance, this other current had the soul irradiated by Someone else and made his seat - the soul that is in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed: that a person striving to be God's friend shall truly see the good things of heaven, the Spirit of the Lord making himself for worthy souls their rest, their rejoicing, their delight.

And it was honest about what that does not fix. Mere abstention from evil things is not perfection - the serpent lies under the mind, beneath the surface of the thoughts, for the heart is a deep gulf. Someone was once asked what becomes of a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing, but to hate it, is.

So yes: the heart connects to grace the way a room connects to light that comes from outside it - not as something the heart produces, but as something the heart receives and is changed by, while still carrying the struggle it had before.
